original_value: Surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonators are low cost devices that can operate wirelessly on a received radio frequency (RF) signal with no requirement for an additional power source. Multiple SAW resonators operating as transponders that form a wireless sensor network (WSN), often need to operate at tightly spaced, different frequencies inside the industrial, scientific and medical (ISM) bands. This requires nanometer precision in the design and fabrication processes. Here, we present results demonstrating a reliable and repeatable fabrication process that yields at least four arrays on a single 4-inch wafer. Each array consists of four single-port resonators with center frequencies allocated inside four different sub-bands that have less than 50 kHz bandwidth and quality factors exceeding 8000. We see promise of standard, low-cost photolithography techniques being used to fabricate multiple SAW resonators with different center resonances all inside the 433.05 MHz–434.79 MHz ISM band and a mere 100 kHz spacing. We achieved that by leveraging the intrinsic process variation of photolithography and the impact of the metallization ratio and metal thickness in rendering distinct resonant frequencies.

result.paraphrase: Surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonators are inexpensive devices that can run wirelessly from a received radio frequency (RF) signal without needing any extra power source. When multiple SAW resonators act as transponders in a wireless sensor network (WSN), they often must operate at closely spaced, distinct frequencies within the industrial, scientific and medical (ISM) bands. Meeting this demand calls for nanometer-level precision during design and fabrication. Here, we present results showing a dependable, repeatable fabrication process that produces at least four arrays on a single 4-inch wafer. Each array contains four single-port resonators whose center frequencies are assigned within four separate sub-bands, each under 50 kHz wide and with quality factors above 8000. We see potential for standard, low-cost photolithography to fabricate multiple SAW resonators with different center resonances, all within the 433.05 MHz–434.79 MHz ISM band and spaced by just 100 kHz. This was achieved by taking advantage of the inherent process variation in photolithography and the effects of metallization ratio and metal thickness on producing distinct resonant frequencies.
